title: Dependency Upgrade Readiness
decision: For a named dependency and candidate version, decide whether to adopt, hold, or replace it before a release. Report exact-version compatibility evidence, required migration work, support status, security advisories, contradictions, and the smallest local verification plan; never claim the project passed tests that were not run.

preferred: the dependency maintainer's versioned release notes, migration guides, and compatibility matrix
official runtime and platform support schedules
package registry metadata and the dependency's first-party repository releases
authoritative security advisories for affected and fixed version ranges
excluded: unlinked SEO summaries and unofficial fork releases
access-control bypasses or executing package code during research

deliverables: adopt, hold, or replace decision with evidence-backed rationale
compatibility matrix naming current and candidate versions plus supported runtimes
migration steps, affected APIs, support dates, and unresolved contradictions
smallest local build, test, and rollback checks still required
queries: <package> <candidate version> official release notes breaking changes runtime support
<package> <candidate version> migration guide deprecation security advisory

freshness.rationale: Check current support and advisory status from dated official sources; versioned changelogs remain useful for historical changes but cannot prove current support on their own.

invalidation: Recheck if the current or candidate dependency version, resolved lockfile graph, package manager, or application runtime target changes.
Invalidate support and advisory claims if their official source changes or is more than 90 days old.
risks: Upstream compatibility statements do not prove this application builds or behaves correctly; local verification remains required.
Transitive resolution and peer constraints can change the effective dependency graph; state the resolved graph as unknown until the operator installs and inspects it.
Advisory severity alone does not settle upgrade priority; preserve affected ranges, fixed versions, and conflicting guidance.
